method: The GeoJSON is parsed locally into polygons and rings, and each ring must hold at least four positions with the first equal to the last; an unclosed ring is closed automatically and reported in a warning. A point is inside a ring when a ray cast eastwards from the point crosses its edges an odd number of times (even-odd rule), and the crossings of all rings in one polygon are summed so that a point inside a hole has an even count and is reported outside that polygon. Ring longitudes are unwrapped by adding or subtracting 360 degrees between consecutive vertices, then shifted by whole turns to sit near the tested longitude, which makes polygons that cross the antimeridian test correctly on both sides of 180. The point is on the boundary when its distance to the nearest segment is at most 0.01 m. Edge distances are measured in a local tangent plane at the point's latitude: 111,320 m per degree of longitude scaled by the cosine of the latitude and 110,540 m per degree of latitude, taking the perpendicular projection clamped to each segment's endpoints. Coordinates must be decimal-degree latitude and longitude within -90 to 90 and -180 to 180, and positions must be JSON numbers; projected coordinates, shapes spanning a pole, shapes spanning more than half the globe and polygons with more than 20,000 vertices are outside the model. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.
